Maximum likelihood fit of a beta-binomial distribution

Source: R/share_intervals.R
fit_betabinom.Rd

Estimates the mean mu and the concentration kappa of a beta-binomial distribution from counts x out of n, with parametrisation alpha = mu kappa, beta = (1 - mu) kappa.

Usage

fit_betabinom(x, n, mean = NULL)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of counts (non-integer values, e.g. counts divided by a design effect, are allowed).

n

Numeric vector of trials, same length as x or length 1. Rows with n = 0 are dropped.

mean

NULL (default) to estimate the mean, or a known mean: a single value or one value per element of x, in (0, 1). With a known mean only kappa is estimated.

Value

A list with mean (estimated or given mean), kappa (concentration; Inf when the data show no overdispersion), rho (intra-class correlation 1 / (1 + kappa)), loglik (maximised log-likelihood, binomial coefficients included) and convergence (0 on success, as in stats::optim()).

Details

The log-likelihood is sum(lchoose(n, x) + lbeta(x + alpha, n - x + beta) - lbeta(alpha, beta)), with the binomial coefficient computed through lgamma(). With an unknown mean the maximisation runs on (logit(mu), log(kappa)) with stats::optim() (method "L-BFGS-B", kappa in [1e-6, 1e8]); with a known mean it runs on log(kappa) with stats::optimize().

When the maximum is reached at the upper bound of kappa the data are compatible with a binomial distribution: the function then returns kappa = Inf, rho = 0, the binomial log-likelihood and a warning. A warning and kappa = Inf are also returned when all counts are 0 or all equal n and the mean is unknown.

Examples

set.seed(1)
p <- stats::rbeta(40, 2, 18)
x <- stats::rbinom(40, 500, p)
fit_betabinom(x, 500)
#> $mean
#> [1] 0.1094461
#> 
#> $kappa
#> [1] 21.47674
#> 
#> $rho
#> [1] 0.04449043
#> 
#> $loglik
#> [1] -192.8856
#> 
#> $convergence
#> [1] 0
#> 
fit_betabinom(x, 500, mean = 0.1)
#> $mean
#> [1] 0.1
#> 
#> $kappa
#> [1] 22.78952
#> 
#> $rho
#> [1] 0.04203532
#> 
#> $loglik
#> [1] -193.3201
#> 
#> $convergence
#> [1] 0
#>
